newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians doubt accord on verge of conclusion.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians doubt accord on verge of conclusion.

text.p: PLO officials said they were unlikely to finalise an agreement with Israel on a Hebron withdrawal on Monday despite intense efforts to reach a conclusion.
"Most probably we will not be able to conclude the drafting tonight but we will continue working until we do," one official told Reuters.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross was meeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at his office in parliament before Israeli and Palestinian negotiators reconvened in Jerusalem from a four-hour recess.
Netanyahu's cabinet secretary Danny Naveh said early in the day a deal could be concluded on Monday, but later he said: "There is still much work ahead."
Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erakat expressed dismay at Israeli statements about the difficulties in the talks.

"We are having problems but we are trying hard to overcome them," he told Reuters. "I am astonished at Israeli statements that the Palestinians are trying to reopen agreed issues because this does not help the process. Quite the opposite happened today."

An Israeli handover of 80 percent of Hebron has seemed within reach many times in recent months but concerns for the security of the West Bank town's 400 Jews and 100,000 Arabs -- along with other issues -- have delayed an agreement.

Mediation on Sunday by Jordan's King Hussein removed a key negotiating block. Under the compromise -- proposed by both Egypt and Jordan -- Israel will complete three troop withdrawals from other, mostly rural occupied West Bank areas by mid-1998.
The PLO had been reluctant to sign an accord without a commitment from Israel to carry out the additional West Bank pullbacks agreed in previous peace deals.
Palestinian negotiators left Monday's talks at a Jerusalem hotel to report to President Yasser Arafat in the self-ruled Gaza Strip. They were due to return to the hotel later in the day.
U.S. envoy Ross, buoyed by the progress, reversed his plans to head home on Sunday and acted as mediator.
Erekat said: "We are trying now to make sure we go over every word, every article of the agreement."

In Washington, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said President Bill Clinton had telephoned Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday "to exchange views with him on the status of the dialogue" and get Mubarak's insights "into the thinking of those who are negotiating".
Cautioning reporters against being over-optimistic, McCurry said: "This is a process that requires hard work. Some progress has been made but there are differences that remain between the parties."
News of an imminent agreement angered members of Netanyahu's right-wing cabinet and Jewish settler leaders who want to hold on to the lands occupied since the 1967 Middle East war.

At least seven ministers in Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet were expected to oppose the deal. Jewish settlers warned the handover would lead to bloodshed in the town holy to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
